Open Library Public Domain Opportunity Radar¶

1 Executive Summary¶

This report screens the full Open Library catalogue, 41.7 million works and 56.9 million editions as of 31 October 2026, for books that are, or will become on 1 January 2027, free to republish in the United States (publication-based terms) and the Philippines (author's life + 50 years). It then measures reader demand (13.2 million reading-log entries and 1.07 million ratings) and current supply (recent editions, publishers, scans and Filipino-language editions). All processing ran in PySpark, and the cleaned tables were saved as Parquet.

Main findings

  • 6.06 million works (14.5%) are potentially public domain under at least one of the two rules. 1.51 million of them are free only under the Philippine rule, which confirms that life + 50 releases many 20th-century works decades before the US does. Examples include Think and Grow Rich, How to Win Friends and Influence People, The Hobbit and Animal Farm.
  • 96,544 works enter the public domain on 1 January 2027: 71,520 first published in 1931 (US), 24,888 whose last author died in 1976 (Philippines) and 136 under both rules. In the Philippines this group is dominated by Agatha Christie (died 1976): 1,012 catalogued works carrying 22,008 Want-to-Read entries, 52% of all demand among 2027 entrants, and none has a Filipino-language edition.
  • Readers want older works about as much as newer ones: the mean rating is close to 4.0 stars in every rights group. Want-to-Read entries fell in the most recent 12 months in every group, but least for public-domain works (−5.7% against −31.7% for post-1978 works), so their share of demand rose from 5.1% to 6.7%.
  • Supply is thin and almost entirely non-Filipino. Only 1.8% of US public-domain works have an edition from 2017 onwards, and only 4,252 of 41.7 million works (0.01%) have any edition in Tagalog or Filipino.
  • The 2027 watchlist keeps 53 works with at least 33 Want-to-Read entries (the top 1% of shelved works) and at most one edition since 2017. It is led by Joy of Cooking (1931 text), Josef Albers's Interaction of Colour and Dalton Trumbo's Johnny Got His Gun.

Caveats. Only 3.7% of authors have a known death year, so 84% of works cannot be classified under the Philippine rule. Some first-publication years and author links are wrong. For example, Light in August is catalogued as 1931 but was published in 1932, and a modern Robert Greene title inherits the death year of the Elizabethan dramatist (1592). We therefore flag suspicious cases rather than hide them, and treat every list as a shortlist for verification, not legal advice. All ten independent recounts of the published totals matched.

2 Introduction¶

When a book enters the public domain, anyone may reprint, translate, adapt or digitize it without asking permission or paying royalties. For a publisher this is a recurring, predictable opportunity: every 1 January a new group of works becomes free to use. In the United States, books first published in 1931 enter the public domain on 1 January 2027. In the Philippines the term is based on the author's life rather than the publication date: protection lasts for the author's life plus 50 years, so works by an author who died in 1976 become free on the same day, and some works that are still protected in the United States or Europe may already be free in the Philippines.

Finding these opportunities is still largely manual. An editor has to check when a book first appeared, when every author died, whether readers still want it, and whether other publishers already keep it in print. This project automates that first screening step with the monthly bulk data published by Open Library, a free, editable library catalogue run by the Internet Archive.

Objectives (from the accepted game plan)

  1. Estimate copyright status from first-publication years and author death dates, and flag works that are potentially public domain.
  2. Analyze reading-log shelf counts, ratings and Want-to-Read trends.
  3. Count recent editions, publishers, digitized copies and Filipino-language editions.
  4. Create a 2027 watchlist of high-demand, low-supply works and a list of works that are potentially public domain.

Scope. We use the October 2026 dumps of works, editions, authors, Wikidata links, reading logs and ratings, processed with PySpark and saved as Parquet. The analysis is descriptive (counts, shares, aggregations and charts); there is no predictive model. Covers, lists and revision history are excluded. Rights classifications are estimates, not legal advice, and reading activity reflects Open Library users only.

3 Data Description¶

We use six of the monthly dumps dated 31 October 2026 (downloaded from the Internet Archive mirror and checked against its published MD5 checksums). Together they hold 18.5 GB of compressed text; after parsing only the fields we need, the Parquet tables take 3.2 GB.

Dump Compressed Records kept What one record is Fields used
works 4.08 GB 41,731,960 an abstract book (all its editions) title, author keys, first publish date, subjects
editions 12.63 GB 56,900,885 one published edition work key, publish date, publishers, languages, Internet Archive scan id (ocaid)
authors 0.78 GB 15,474,645 a person or organization name, birth and death dates (free text), Wikidata id
wikidata 0.83 GB 169,128 a Wikidata item linked to Open Library birth (P569), death (P570), Open Library id (P648), citizenship (P27)
reading-log 0.13 GB 13,218,055 one book on a reader's shelf work, shelf, date logged
ratings 0.01 GB 1,069,316 one star rating work, rating (1-5), date

Some properties of the data shape every result that follows (full coverage table in Section 4.2):

  • Publication years come mostly from editions. Only 10.6% of works carry their own first_publish_date, but 96.7% of editions have a parseable year, so we can date 96.3% of works.
  • Death years are rare. Only 3.6% of Open Library authors have a usable death_date, and 1.2% link to Wikidata. This is the main limit on the Philippine (life-based) estimates.
  • Demand is concentrated. 10.9 million Want-to-Read entries fall on just 2.9 million works (7.0% of the catalogue); ratings are skewed towards 4 stars (56% of ratings, mean 4.0).
  • Reading-log dates run from October 2017 to October 2026, so trends can be described over nine years.

Following the course rules, no raw or processed data is included with this report; the notebook rebuilds everything from the dumps.

4 Methodology¶

All processing code lives in helper_code.py, which this notebook imports. Each function there has a docstring that explains its inputs, outputs and assumptions, and the companion notebook TEST.ipynb checks those functions on small hand-made examples whose answers were worked out by hand (43 tests, including every copyright boundary year). This notebook only calls the functions in order and discusses what they return, so it can be run from top to bottom (Kernel > Restart & Run All).

4.1 Setup and ingestion with PySpark¶

Open Library publishes each dump as one gzip-compressed text file. Five of the six files share a layout of five tab-separated columns (record type, key, revision, last-modified time and the record itself as JSON); the Wikidata file stores each Wikidata item's JSON in CSV-style quotes, and the reading-log and ratings files are plain tab-separated tables.

For each dump, build_parquet_tables reads the lines as text, splits the columns and parses only the JSON fields we need with an explicit schema (works_schema, editions_schema, and so on). Declaring the schema has three benefits: Spark does not scan the file to guess types, the output has the same columns every month, and fields we never use (for example table-of-contents text) are skipped instead of being loaded into memory. The cleaned tables are saved as Parquet, a compressed column format that later steps can read in parallel and in seconds.

Two practical details shape this step. First, a gzip file cannot be split, so Spark must read each dump with a single task; we therefore submit the six dumps as concurrent Spark jobs so that the cores work on different files at the same time. Second, each table is written once and reused: if its Parquet folder is complete, a later run of this notebook skips the parsing. The first run takes about an hour on a 4-core machine because of the 12.6 GB editions file; later runs take minutes. Once a table's Parquet folder is complete, its raw dump is no longer needed. In our run we deleted the two largest raw files (works and editions) after checking that the editions table held exactly as many records as the raw file had lines (56,900,885), because Spark needs free disk space for the temporary "shuffle" files it writes during large joins. The inventory below therefore shows those two files as not present.

To run the notebook, place the ol_dump_*.txt.gz files in a data/ folder next to it (or set the OL_DATA_DIR environment variable). The dumps are listed at https://openlibrary.org/developers/dumps and mirrored on the Internet Archive as ol_dump_YYYY-MM-DD.

def show(table, title=None, rows=10, index=False, floats=2):
    # Display the first rows of a table as compact, wrapped HTML.
    if title:
        print(title)
    if table is None or len(table) == 0:
        print("No rows meet the stated selection criteria.")
        return
    html = table.head(rows).to_html(
        index=index, border=0, na_rep="-",
        float_format=lambda v: f"{v:,.{floats}f}",
    )
    display(HTML('<div style="overflow-x:auto;max-width:1100px">'
                 + html + "</div>"))

4.2 Data quality¶

Before using a field we measure how often it is present and usable, because a missing value can change a rights estimate. For example, a work without any dated edition has no first-publication year, so its US status must be "unknown" rather than "protected". profile_tables counts, in one pass per table, the rows whose JSON parsed, the rows with each field, and the rows from whose free-text dates a valid year could be extracted.

Years are extracted with a simple, documented rule: the first four-digit number between 1450 and 2026 in the text (so "February 27, 1997" gives 1997, "c1931" gives 1931, and "19--" gives no year). Author birth and death dates use a slightly different rule: they keep the latest year in the text (so "1850 or 1851" gives 1851), because a later death means longer protection, and the estimate should err towards "still in copyright". find_duplicate_keys checks that every work, edition and author key appears only once, since a duplicate would be double-counted in every later join.

duplicates = helper.find_duplicate_keys(tables)

show(duplicates, "Keys that appear more than once")

4.3 Author death years: Open Library and Wikidata¶

Life-based copyright terms need the death year of every author of a work. Open Library's own death_date field is free text and often empty, so we add structured dates from Wikidata (property P570, date of death). An author is linked to a Wikidata item in either direction: through the author record's remote_ids.wikidata value, or through a Wikidata item whose property P648 lists the author's Open Library ID. Values that Wikidata marks as deprecated (known to be wrong) and dates less precise than a year (for example "1900s") are ignored. When several items or values remain, the latest death year is used.

When both sources give a year, Wikidata is preferred because it is typed and usually referenced. The agreement table below measures how often the two sources agree; the last row counts authors whose Philippine status would change depending on which source we trusted, which shows how much this choice matters for the results. Wikidata's country of citizenship (P27 = Q928, Philippines) is also kept to identify Filipino authors.

4.4 Estimating copyright status¶

We estimate each work's status on 1 January 2027 under two legal regimes, using the rules summarized below (and implemented in us_status and life_plus_status).

Regime Basis Public domain on 1 Jan 2027 Enters on 1 Jan 2027 Uncertain or protected
United States (17 U.S.C. sec. 302-304) first publication year Y; 95-year term for works published before 1978 Y ≤ 1930 Y = 1931 1932-1963: PD only if the copyright was not renewed (renewal records are not in Open Library); 1964 onwards: protected
Philippines (RA 8293, sec. 213-214) death year D of the last surviving author; life + 50 years D ≤ 1975 D = 1976 D ≥ 1977 protected; any author without a death year: unknown
Life + 70 (EU, UK and others), for comparison as above, life + 70 D ≤ 1955 D = 1956 D ≥ 1957 protected

A work's first-publication year is the earlier of the work record's first_publish_date and its earliest dated edition. This is how Open Library itself reports "first published", but one mis-dated edition can make a work look older than it is. Two checks guard against this:

  • year_before_birth: the first year is earlier than the last author's birth year plus 10, which is implausible for a genuine first edition. These works are kept in the counts but flagged and excluded from every list.
  • gap_after_death: the first year is more than 70 years after the last author's death, which suggests that the catalogue lacks the older editions. These works are probably older (and freer) than estimated.

A work is called potentially public domain if it is unflagged and public domain under the US rule or the Philippine rule, and it enters in 2027 if it is unflagged and enters under either rule.

4.5 Demand: reading log and ratings¶

Open Library readers can put a work on one of three shelves: Want to Read, Currently Reading or Already Read, and they can rate it from one to five stars. The dumps contain one row per shelf entry or rating, with the date it was made, but no user identifier. compute_demand therefore counts entries per work: Want-to-Read entries are our main demand signal, because they record books people intend to read but may not yet have.

To describe trends, we count Want-to-Read entries made in the 12 months to 31 October 2026 and in the 12 months before that, and we chart monthly entries for each rights group. One caution applies throughout: the dump only holds entries that are still on a shelf, so when a reader finishes or removes a book, its older Want-to-Read entry disappears. Older months are therefore undercounted, and an upward slope partly reflects this survivorship rather than growing interest.

In [6]:

shelf_summary = helper.summarize_shelves(tables["reading_log"],
                                         tables["ratings"])

show(shelf_summary["ratings"], "Ratings by star value")

4.6 Supply: editions, publishers, scans and Filipino editions¶

For each work, compute_supply summarizes its editions:

  • Editions and recent editions (published 2017-2026, the ten years up to the dump). A work that many publishers keep reissuing is already well served; a wanted work with no recent edition is an opening.
  • Publishers and recent publishers, counted after normalizing names (lower case, punctuation removed, legal suffixes such as "Ltd." dropped), so "Penguin Books Ltd." and "Penguin Books" count once.
  • Digitized copies: editions with an Internet Archive scan (ocaid), which signal that a free digital copy may already exist.
  • Filipino-language editions: editions catalogued with the language codes tgl (Tagalog) or fil (Filipino), the gap a Philippine translation could fill.

Editions without a valid year are counted as editions but never as recent, so recent counts are lower bounds. Rights status, demand and supply are then joined into one work profile row per work, with zero counts (not missing values) for works nobody has shelved.

In [7]:
supply = helper.compute_supply(tables["editions"])
profile = helper.materialize(
    spark, helper.build_work_profile(status, demand, supply),
    PARQUET_DIR / "work_profile",
)
print(f"Work profile: {profile.count():,} works x "
      f"{len(profile.columns)} columns")

Work profile: 41,731,960 works x 38 columns

4.7 Watchlist and public-domain list¶

The 2027 watchlist keeps works that meet all three conditions:

  1. they enter the public domain on 1 January 2027 under the US rule (first published 1931) or the Philippine rule (last author died 1976), with no data-quality flag;
  2. they are in high demand: their Want-to-Read count is at least the 99th percentile among all works with at least one entry (most works in the catalogue have none, so a percentile over all works would be zero);
  3. they have low recent supply: at most one edition since 2017.

The list is ranked by Want-to-Read entries, then by entries in the last 12 months, then by number of ratings. The potentially public domain list applies the same demand threshold to works that are already free under either rule. Both cut-offs are judgement calls, so Section 5.4 also reports how the watchlist changes under other reasonable choices.

In [8]:
WTR_QUANTILE = 0.99          # "high demand" = top 1% of shelved works
MAX_RECENT_EDITIONS = 1      # "low supply" = at most one edition since 2017
min_wtr = helper.demand_threshold(profile, WTR_QUANTILE)

watchlist_all = helper.build_watchlist(profile, min_wtr,
                                       MAX_RECENT_EDITIONS)
watchlist = helper.build_watchlist(profile, min_wtr, MAX_RECENT_EDITIONS,
                                   top_n=50, authors=tables["authors"])
pd_list = helper.build_pd_list(profile, min_want_to_read=min_wtr,
                               top_n=50, authors=tables["authors"])
print(f"High-demand threshold: at least {min_wtr} Want-to-Read entries "
      f"(the {WTR_QUANTILE:.0%} quantile among works with any entry)")
print(f"Works on the 2027 watchlist: {watchlist_all.count():,}")

High-demand threshold: at least 33 Want-to-Read entries (the 99% quantile among works with any entry)

4.8 Computational validation¶

Aggregations over tens of millions of rows can fail silently, for example when a join drops rows or duplicates them. validate_analysis recounts key totals along a different code path and compares the two answers: for instance, the number of editions attached to known works is counted directly from the editions table and compared with the sum of the per-work edition counts. It also re-applies the Python versions of the US and Philippine rules to a random 0.1% sample of works and checks that Spark assigned exactly the same status.

In [9]:
validation = helper.validate_analysis(
    tables, status, profile, watchlist_all, min_wtr, MAX_RECENT_EDITIONS)
show(validation, "Independent recounts", rows=20)
print(f"{int(validation['passed'].sum())} of {len(validation)} checks "
      "passed")

5 Results and Discussion¶

5.1 How much of the catalogue is, or will be, public domain?¶

Under the US rule, 4.61 million works (11.1%) were first published in 1930 or earlier and are already public domain. Another 71,810 (0.2%) date from 1931 and enter on 1 January 2027. A further 3.01 million (7.2%) are in the 1932-1963 "renewal unknown" window: many of these are probably free, because most copyrights from that period were never renewed, but the dumps cannot tell us which. Most of the catalogue (69.2%) was first published in 1978 or later.

The Philippine rule gives a very different picture, mostly because of missing data. 84.1% of works have at least one author without a death year and 5.5% have no linked author, so only 10.4% can be classified at all. Of those, most are already free (3.42 million works, 8.2% of the catalogue), 903,403 are protected, and 25,129 enter in 2027.

The cross-tabulation below shows where the two regimes disagree. 1.51 million works are public domain in the Philippines but not clearly so in the US, including 764,857 first published after 1977, typically posthumous editions or translations of authors who died long ago. In the other direction, 15,215 works published in 1930 or earlier are still protected in the Philippines because one of their authors died after 1976 (for example a modern translator or editor credited as an author). This is the gap the game plan anticipated: each country's rule frees a different set of works, and the life-based rule frees some much earlier.

The histogram of first-publication years (log scale) shows the steady growth of publishing, with colours marking the US groups. Two spikes are data artefacts rather than history: 131,598 works are dated exactly 1900 (about twice the neighbouring years) and 26,149 exactly 1800, which look like placeholder dates used by some catalogue sources. Both are before 1931, so the affected works count as public domain in the US; if their real dates are later, this group is overstated.

Three data-quality flags quantify the remaining uncertainty:

  • 72,390 works have a first year earlier than their author's birth plus 10 years (year_before_birth), and 4,697 have authors with impossible life dates. These 0.2% are flagged and excluded from every list.
  • 950,690 works were first catalogued more than 70 years after their last author died (gap_after_death). Most are classics whose early editions are simply missing (The Art of War, Meditations). Some, however, are modern books linked to the wrong, much older author. Section 5.5 measures how often this affects the lists.

5.2 Reading activity and Want-to-Read trends¶

Older works are shelved less often per work than new ones. 3.5% of public-domain works have at least one Want-to-Read entry, compared with 8.1% of post-1978 works. But because the public-domain group is large, it still collects 586,358 Want-to-Read entries, and the 1932-1963 group another 688,552. Ratings are almost identical across groups (mean 3.9-4.1 stars). A reader who finds an older book is about as satisfied as one reading a recent title, so age itself does not signal weak demand.

In [12]:

show(groups[["US status", "works", "pct_with_wtr", "mean_wtr",

The monthly chart shows four features that matter for interpreting trends:

  1. Activity grows from 2022. Monthly entries rise severalfold in every group between 2021 and 2023, in step with Open Library's overall growth, so raw growth mostly reflects more users rather than more interest in particular books.
  2. A sharp dip in October 2024 appears in all four groups at once. It coincides with the period when the Internet Archive, which runs Open Library, was offline after a cyber-attack, so it reflects service availability, not reader interest.
  3. The last month is the highest. Entries made recently have had the least time to be removed from shelves, so recent months are inflated relative to older ones (the survivorship effect described in 4.5).
  4. Group spikes. The public-domain line has an isolated spike in May 2023 that does not appear elsewhere. A single popular list or import is the likeliest cause, so we do not read it as a trend.

Comparing the last 12 months with the 12 before, entries fell in every group, but by very different amounts: −5.7% for US public-domain works against −31.7% for post-1978 works. As a result, public-domain works rose from 5.1% to 6.7% of all Want-to-Read activity. Both windows are equally affected by the outage dip (it falls in the earlier window) and by survivorship (which favours the later window), so the relative change between groups is more trustworthy than the absolute decline.

  • Recent editions are rare for older works. Only 1.8% of US public-domain works, 0.8% of 1931 works and 0.8% of 1932-1963 works have an edition dated 2017 or later, compared with 28.7% of post-1978 works. Most old works are effectively out of print in the catalogue.
  • Scans are common for older works. 31.5% of public-domain works have an Internet Archive scan, roughly three times the rate for post-1978 works. A scan does not mean the book is free to read online, though: in-copyright scans are only lent, one reader at a time.
  • Filipino-language editions are almost absent. Across the whole catalogue only 4,252 works (4,619 editions) are catalogued in Tagalog or Filipino, about 0.01% in every group. Part of this is under-cataloguing of Philippine publishers in Open Library, but the gap is large enough to suggest a real shortage of Filipino editions of world literature.

The demand-supply grid restricts attention to works that are potentially public domain or enter in 2027. Of the 794 such works with 100 or more Want-to-Read entries, 203 have no edition since 2017 (3 of them with over 1,000 entries). These are the clearest "wanted but not reissued" cases. The grid also shows that the most-wanted public-domain works usually do have many recent editions (62 of the 69 works with 1,000+ entries have ten or more), so the opportunity lies in the less famous middle of the demand distribution.

5.4 The 2027 watchlist¶

96,544 unflagged works enter the public domain on 1 January 2027. Only 6.0% of them have any Want-to-Read entry, and 98% have no edition since 2017, so demand is the selective criterion. The 53-work watchlist splits into 36 works that enter through the Philippine rule (last author died 1976) and 17 through the US rule (published 1931). Of the 53, 42 have no edition since 2017 and none has a Filipino edition. 52 have an Internet Archive scan, so a digitized source text is usually available to work from.

Reading the watchlist. Each row is a lead, and checking the top entries against standard bibliographies shows why it must be verified:

  • Joy of Cooking (Irma S. Rombauer, 1931) is the most-wanted entrant. Only the original 1931 text enters the US public domain; the many later revisions by her co-authors remain protected.
  • Interaction of Colour, Johnny Got His Gun, Call It Courage, Heisenberg's Physics and Philosophy and Auntie Mame enter through the Philippine rule. Their authors (Albers, Trumbo, Sperry, Heisenberg, Patrick Dennis) all died in 1976. In the US these works are either protected or depend on an unchecked renewal.
  • Light in August is a false positive. Open Library's earliest edition is dated 1931, but the novel was published in 1932, so it enters the US public domain in 2028. Cours de linguistique générale (1916) is the reverse case: it is listed as 1931 but is already free.
  • The laws of human nature (R. H. Wheeler, 1931) gained 82 of its 171 entries in the last year. That pattern suggests readers confusing it with Robert Greene's 2018 bestseller of almost the same title, so its demand is probably overstated.
  • Savage Surrender (credited to Pamela Clare, died 1976 according to the catalogue) appears to merge two different authors and needs checking before any decision.

The table of authors shows how concentrated the 2027 opportunity is. Agatha Christie alone accounts for 1,012 entering works and 22,008 Want-to-Read entries, more than every other entrant combined. In the Philippines all of her works become free on 1 January 2027. Elsewhere most stay protected much longer: until 2047 under life + 70, and in the US for 95 years from publication (only her books published in 1931 or earlier are free there). Other 1976 deaths with sizeable catalogues are Benjamin Graham (28 works), Martin Heidegger (722), Paul Gallico (84), Josef Albers (81), Lin Yutang (441) and Samuel Eliot Morison (393). Almost all of their works lack recent editions in the catalogue, and none of Christie's has a Filipino edition.

Sensitivity. The cut-offs change the size of the list but not its top. Relaxing the demand threshold to the 95th percentile (9 entries) gives 283 works, and to the 90th percentile (5 entries) gives 625. Allowing up to five recent editions adds only 27 works at the 99th percentile (53 to 80). The low-supply condition is not the binding constraint, because almost no 2027 entrant has been reissued recently.

5.5 Works that are potentially public domain already¶

The second deliverable lists works that are potentially public domain already, with the same demand threshold (at least 33 Want-to-Read entries); 2,352 works qualify. The most wanted of them are dominated by works that are free only under the Philippine rule (US status "renewal": published 1932-1963): Think and Grow Rich (Napoleon Hill, died 1970, 16,158 entries), How to Win Friends and Influence People (Dale Carnegie, died 1955), The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings (Tolkien, died 1973), Animal Farm (Orwell, died 1950), Le Petit Prince (Saint-Exupéry, died 1944) and No Longer Human (Dazai, died 1948). Most of these already have dozens of recent editions, so they are crowded markets. The second table applies the low-supply filter as well.

The low-supply view (1,245 works) surfaces less obvious leads: Eric Berne's Games People Play (1,881 entries, no edition since 2017; free in the Philippines since Berne died in 1970), Tan Malaka's Madilog (1,084 entries) and several C. S. Lewis titles (died 1963). It also shows the two main failure modes of the estimates:

  • Wrong author link. Las 48 leyes del poder (Robert Greene, 1998) appears because its author record carries the death year of the Elizabethan writer Robert Greene (1592). It is a false positive, and it is marked by gap_after_death. This warning fires on 11.4% of the high-demand public-domain list and 14.4% of its low-supply subset, but on only 1 of the 146 high-demand 2027 entrants. Every flagged row needs its author checked before use.
  • Duplicate work records. Classics such as The Wealth of Nations or Paradise Lost show hundreds of editions but none since 2017. Open Library often splits one title across several work records, and recent editions attached to a duplicate are not counted, so "low supply" is least reliable for very famous titles.

Finally, only 78 authors in the Wikidata dump are marked as Philippine citizens. Their 1,190 catalogued works include 513 already free in the Philippines, but they carry few reading-log entries. Philippine authors are under-represented in both Wikidata links and Open Library activity, so this analysis cannot yet measure local demand for local classics.

5.6 Limitations¶

  • Missing and wrong death years. Only 3.7% of authors have a death year, so 84% of works are "unknown" under the life-based rule. Where Open Library and Wikidata both give a year they agree for 98.8% of authors (within one year), and only 75 authors would change Philippine status depending on the source. Errors therefore come mainly from wrong links between works and authors, which no single-source check can detect.
  • Publication years. First years come from the earliest catalogued edition. They can be too early (a misdated edition, as with Light in August), too late (old editions missing, 950,690 works), or placeholders (the 1900 and 1800 spikes).
  • US renewals. The 3.0 million works first published 1932-1963 cannot be classified without US Copyright Office renewal records, which are not in the dumps. We also ignore special US cases: works by US government authors (always public domain), works published without a copyright notice before 1978, and foreign works whose US copyright was restored in 1996.
  • Philippine law. We apply only the general life + 50 rule (RA 8293 sec. 213-214). We do not model works of corporate or anonymous authorship, works published after the author's death, or the separate rights of translators and editors. A new translation must start from a source text that is itself free.
  • Work-level counts. A "work" bundles all its editions and translations. Revised editions (Joy of Cooking) and compilations (Christie omnibus volumes) add new material that may still be protected. Duplicate work records split editions and understate supply.
  • Demand. Reading-log and rating activity reflects Open Library users only, who are not representative of all readers (and certainly not of Philippine readers). The dump keeps only entries still on a shelf, undercounting older months, and the October 2024 outage depresses one month.
  • Scope. The analysis is descriptive. The thresholds (99th percentile of demand, at most one recent edition) are judgement calls whose effect we report in Section 5.4, and no estimate here is legal advice.

5.7 Recommendations¶

  1. Act on the Philippine 2027 opportunity first. The clearest lead is the Agatha Christie catalogue, which enters the public domain in the Philippines on 1 January 2027 with substantial demand and no Filipino editions. Working from the original English texts (not later translations or revised compilations), a Philippine publisher could prepare Tagalog or Filipino translations of the most-wanted titles, after legal confirmation of the date of death and of the local term.
  2. Verify each watchlist row before acting. Check the first edition against a national bibliography (this catches cases such as Light in August), confirm the author's identity and death date, and inspect any row marked gap_after_death. The 53-work list is short enough to check by hand in a few days.
  3. Resolve the 1932-1963 renewal question. Matching these 3.0 million works against digitized US renewal records, for example Stanford's Copyright Renewal Database of books from 1923-1963, would turn the largest "uncertain" group into firm answers. That is the most valuable extension of this pipeline.
  4. Improve author dates at the source. Because the Philippine estimate is limited mainly by missing death years and mislinked authors, adding Wikidata links to the most-shelved Open Library authors (and fixing the conflations found here) would raise coverage for everyone using the data.
  5. Re-run monthly. The pipeline reuses its Parquet tables, so each new dump can refresh the lists in about an hour. In late 2027 the same code, with REFERENCE_DATE set to 2028, produces the next year's watchlist (works from 1932 and deaths in 1977).
